passages.happening:
“Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat!” (verse 1). “Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!” (verse 1).

‘Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy?’ (verse 2). They are to listen carefully and eat what is good, and their souls will delight in rich food (verse 2).

‘Incline your ear and come to Me; listen, so that your soul may live’ (verse 3). God will make with them an everlasting covenant, his loving devotion promised to David (verse 3). He made David a witness to the nations, a leader of the peoples (verse 4). Now they will call nations they do not know, and those nations will run to them, because the LORD has given them glory (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 55 closes the great section that began in chapter 40 with God's word of comfort to his people. Chapter 53 showed the Servant bearing sin. Chapter 54 showed Zion restored as a mother of many. Now the invitation goes out to anyone who will come.

Verse 1 sounds like a street seller calling out in a market: water, grain, wine and milk, the basic food of the land. Wine and milk together meant plenty. The surprise is that the seller asks nothing. In a world where most people lived near hunger and spent their labor to buy bread, food without cost was startling.

The question of verse 2 may have had a sharp edge. Many exiles had settled in Babylon, as Jeremiah had told them to, and records show Judeans doing business and holding land there. Comfort in Babylon was set against the call to go home to ruins.

The promise to David came to a people with no king. Zedekiah had been blinded and taken to Babylon, and Jehoiachin was released from prison but never restored. God had promised David a house and a throne forever. Verse 3 says that loyal love still stands, and now it is offered to all who come. Scholars discuss whether this hands the promise to the whole people or renews it in hope of a coming king.
passages.later: God promised David, ‘Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me’ (2 Samuel 7:16). Paul quotes verse 3 in the Greek form, ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David’ (Acts 13:34), as fulfilled when God raised Jesus from the dead.
passages.asks: God asks why people spend their money on what does not satisfy. Ask where your money and labor go, and whether it feeds you. And ask what it means to come to God with nothing to pay.

passages.t: Seek the LORD, and a word that does not return empty
passages.happening:
‘Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near’ (verse 6). ‘Let the wicked man forsake his own way and the unrighteous man his own thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion, and to our God, for He will freely pardon’ (verse 7).

The LORD says that his thoughts are not their thoughts, nor his ways their ways (verse 8). ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts’ (verse 9).

‘For just as rain and snow fall from heaven and do not return without watering the earth’ (verse 10), making it sprout and giving seed and bread, so it is with God's word. ‘So My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty’ (verse 11).

‘You will indeed go out with joy and be led forth in peace’ (verse 12). The mountains will sing and the trees clap their hands. Cypress will grow instead of thornbush and myrtle instead of brier, an everlasting sign for the LORD (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The word for pardon in verse 7, salach, has only God as its subject in the Old Testament. People forgive each other with other words. Here it is strengthened: God will pardon abundantly.

Verses 8 and 9 come straight after that promise. God's thoughts are higher than human thoughts above all in his readiness to forgive, which outruns human ideas of fairness and payback.

Rain and snow were not background weather in Israel. The land depended on the early rains of autumn and the late rains of spring, and a failed rain meant famine. Farmers who watched the sky knew rain does not go back up until it has done its work.

Thornbush and brier were signs of a cursed, neglected land. Their replacement by cypress and myrtle signals the curse reversed. The section began with God's word that stands forever (40:8) and ends with God's word that does not return empty.
passages.later: The section's first promise was, ‘the word of our God stands forever’ (Isaiah 40:8), and the thorns of verse 13 reach back to the curse: ‘Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you’ (Genesis 3:18). A psalm calls creation to the same joy: ‘Let the rivers clap their hands’ (Psalm 98:8).
passages.hard:
If God's thoughts are higher than human thoughts, can anyone really know anything about him?

Verses 8 and 9 are sometimes used to shut down hard questions: God's ways are a mystery, so stop asking. The context points elsewhere. The contrast comes right after verse 7, where the wicked are told God will freely pardon. His thoughts are higher above all in his mercy. And the same passage says his word comes down like rain and does its work, which means he makes himself known.

The church's tradition has held both: God is beyond full human understanding, yet truly known where he shows himself. The verses invite humility, not silence.
passages.asks: God's word comes like rain and does not go back empty. Ask where you have heard God's word and wondered whether anything came of it. And ask what it would take for you to seek the LORD while he is near, today and not later.
